podcast.body: This song became Jerry Lee Lewis's big hit, having been a highlight of his live show. Its authorship is disputed, with both Dave Curly Williams and Roy Hall (credited as Sonny Day David) claiming to have written it; Big Maybelle originally recorded it with an arrangement by Quincy Jones, and Roy Hall also recorded his own version on Decca. Jerry Lee's inspiration came from Johnny Little John, who performed a faster, lead-vocal version with a spoken section at a gig, which Jerry Lee then adopted for his own performances. Initially, Sam Phillips and Jack Clement doubted the song, thinking it too vulgar for radio and too similar to Elvis, preferring "Middle B. Me" as the A-side. However, after several takes during the recording session, which involved Clement and Phillips contributing ideas, lowering the bass in the mix, and adding slapback echo to the piano, the spontaneous-sounding result convinced everyone it had to be the A-side. "When Jerry Lee took his version of the song into Sun, convinced that this was going to be his big hit and neither Sam Phillips nor Jack Clement believed in it."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: This was Jerry Lee Lewis's first really major success, propelling him to the top of the world as the most promising artist in rock and roll music. With Elvis Presley about to be drafted, Lewis intended to take over his mantle as the biggest star. "Holot Shaken was such a massive hit that on the basis of that one record, Jerry Lee was invited to perform his next single in a film called Jamboree."
